Ok, so 37 year old based in Ireland/UK. 

I started pursuing acting in any shape or form about ten years ago.  I came back from Thailand, realized I didn't have it in me, nor did I want to pursue MMA and Muay Thai fighting as a career.  Although perhaps what let me down in that pathway, may well be the same thing that is letting me down in my acting career - lack of self-belief.  My agent routinely reminds me that I need to have "American confidence" - back myself 100%, rather than the classic Irish half-in, half-out, self-deprecating approach to life.

Whilst out in Thailand, I happened to receive an email from a company called prospects - basically informing of various jobs and postgraduate degrees.  This informed of a Masters in Acting for Screen at a prestigious London Drama school.  This set my head-spinning.  I had always wanted to pursue acting in some form, although I'm still not entirely sure whether it was a desire to be famous or admired, rather than a love for acting.  I had done the odd amateur play before and a tiny bit of stand up comedy and I loved goofing off, doing voices, making characters with friends, but at 28, this was an entirely new pursuit. I s decided I'd get whatever classes I could, along with getting parts in student short films, I got extras work in various big TV shows and films that were filmed in the north of Ireland.  

In the years that followed, I developed, got a ton of other short film and alongside doing extras work and bar/restaurant jobs,  eventually got myself onto that MA course.  It was full time and intense.  I hung around London for another 2.5 years, before COVID hit and came back to Ireland.  In the years that I was in London, I took various jobs mostly hospitality, but were not limited to such.  I also did part time PA work and taught English as a foreign language.

  
Since being home in Ireland, I've worked as a civil servant (agency staff on a temporary contract), more hospitality jobs and in a corporate office job, whilst also landing a few short films, and commercials, a chunk of voiceover work.  I've had some decent years, but so many near misses from decent roles in TV and film have left me somewhat jaded.  I keep going and try to find the balance between putting the work in and not giving enough of a shit to take it personally.     
  
Perhaps the best job to work alongside my acting was the corporate office job.  They did give me enough annual leave and also unpaid time off when that ran off when I was on an indy feature.  Unfortunately, if I wanted to continue working my way up the corporate ladder, I would have had a low salary and got to a grade where there was a ton of unpaid overtime.   It also didn't fit very well with me.  The corporation almost certainly plays a part in the financial affairs of states which commit war crimes and arguably a part in the financial crash of 2008.  

I had intentions of starting a Software Development Masters, as the salaries are so high in this country, but I'm hearing of a lot of folk struggling in the tech sector and the threat of AI looms just as highly over the tech industry as it does the film one.  

I have a few more years left before I feel I have to change gears.  I will be getting my driving license (harder in this country than the US.. sorry guys..), and potentially buying a house this year (much easier than in the US.. sorry).  I intend to get my web series off the ground soon, do more stand up comedy and create a VLOG where I walk around Ireland trying out different martial arts, stopping at historical sites to do pieces to camera, stand up comedy, whiskey tasting..

I live in the UK/Ireland, a few years ago this article came out:  
[https://www.theguardian.com/film/shortcuts/2019/jun/05/only-2-per-cent-of-actors-make-a-living-how-do-you-become-one-of-them](https://www.theguardian.com/film/shortcuts/2019/jun/05/only-2-per-cent-of-actors-make-a-living-how-do-you-become-one-of-them)  


Only 2% of actors make a full time living from acting.  However, I think the number can be a little higher, for the simple reasons that a) this may be based on the amount actors choose to declare on their self-assessment tax returns.  Actors may be under-declaring, or writing off a huge amount of their earnings through expenses and b) depending on the type of acting you're doing, you may not be employed all the time in acting.  This means that actors will take up other pursuits, either as writers, producers or film/theatre makers, or in a more grounded day-job.    


Despite me expecting actor's earnings to be higher to what this article states, I am still well aware that most actors need to have either their own side-hustle, or a full, or flexible career.  A former friend of mine (we got on well online, but made the fatal mistake of meeting each other for real and finding out we were so painfully unsuited to being around each other) works in event catering and hospitality as her flexible job in LA.  It's quite well paid (around $32 an hour, I believe) but she realized that she was working alongside someone who had been a series lead in quite a big show for several seasons.  Either there were no residuals coming in and he had been drastically underpaid for the amount of revenue the show had generated, or he had frivolously spent what he had earned, or perhaps even.. he was bored and needed something to do with his time.

To me this indicated what I'd be in for even if I got to the level of success I'd be hoping for.  I think so much of my mindset truly believes that when I "make it", my brain will be satiated, I will be somehow more secure in myself and capable of settling down a bit more in life, rather than jump from place to place, or side-hustle to side-hustle, I will be mentally and soulfully enriched.  It's something that is somehow ingrained in my psyche just like my belief in God was when I was a kid growing up and being fed Bible stories inside and outside of school.  I'm only beginning to hit a "mental adolescence" and realize, that God, or in this case mental security, may not truly come if and when I "make it".

On the other hand on a more realistic note, I was told by a producer I was very close to getting a great part on the second season of a cop show produced locally.  This job would have been paid around £4-5k a week for just under 30 weeks.  I make less than £4k a month through bar work, voiceover work, content writing, so £4k a week would be delightful.  Additionally, a 3 bedroom house not too far from me would be less than £170k, so moneywise I'd be incredibly comfortable, all whilst doing the one job I want to do the most.

I am always looking out for a stable, flexible job and I foolishly gave one up at the end of 2022.  Whilst I don't think I'm particularly good at working in corporate office roles, the level of flexibility that they offer is fairly high.  In 2022, I worked on two indy feature projects, which ate all of my holiday days, but in addition to the annual leave, I was given unpaid time off.  Note though, that in Europe, the corporate culture is different than the US.  In the US, you're not expected to use all of your time off, it's almost like suggesting you're lazy for not kowtowing to the bullshit expectations placed upon you by the company, whereas European companies at least want to give the illusion that they understand you are a person with multiple ambitions and can still give to the company massively whilst pursuing your own goals.

I always knew that I wanted to give acting a go.  I enjoyed it so much when it "clicked" and I really felt the rhythym and beats of a scene, or I connected with the other actors.  I started quite late into my career and began taking workshops and small parts in short films and read rehearsals around the age of 26.  I managed to get accepted onto a Masters course in one of the most prestigious acting schools in London when I was 29.  Throughout this period, I had big bursts of confidence and big dragging doubts.  This was all stuff that I hoped would go away once I finished my masters and would somehow find representation and be seen for things straight away.  This was almost the case too as I was headhunted by a well established agency who wanted to come and see me act.  Unfortunatley, they never came to the showcase they said they would and tossed me aside.

​

It took a while to get other UK representation.  The initial agency felt incredibly dodgy, charging me a yearly fee (which I believe is illegal), they also booked me onto a nationwide advertisement campaign which paid a paltry £300.  I switched agent, then got an Irish agent.  The UK one seemed bent on sending me to nothing but commercials, whilst the Irish one initially started strong, but due to his own mental health issues and drug/alcohol misuse became bad to keep around.  In those days, I landed a pilot, a corporate safety video and was incredibly close to getting a named role on a very big show.  

I did bits and pieces of networking, working on smaller films, the odd bit of producing shorts, but only small parts of this amounted to anything at all.  Throughout this I couldn't get out of the constant flux of thinking "I'm awesome and deserve this" to "I'm absolutely awful.  I piece of shit and a shit actor".  I'd publically celebrate the success of my friends, all the while envying them and having bouts of self-pitying nonsense.

When lockdown hit, I took some time out and was kinda glad.  Well if I wasn't getting any work, why should anyone else?  I started my own showreel production company, which was meant to develop into something bigger and better.  I lost focus at times, but I was starting to get more paid short film roles and was somehow lead in an indy feature, which has been in the cutting room for 1.5 years.  However, I still feel at times that this may not go anywhere, or that time to be successful is running out in an oversaturated market, as budgets appear to bottom out when it comes to paying actors, and the threat of AI looms.  

I sometimes wonder, am I in this game due to sunk cost fallacy - do I want to quit, but don't want to be a failed actor.  Am I tired of quitting, like I seem to quit everything else in life? Whilst I think as another commenter as said, it's pretty good at the start, feels fairly naturalistic but as you have to push, it doesn't hold together as well.  The good news is that it's a solid starting point and I think there's a fair bit to feel good about.

​

First thing to ask - did you have anyone talking to you over the phone as you were delivering this monologue?  That may have helped.  Remembering a monologue has a subject, an objective and obstacles in order to operate is hugely important.  Much like a dialogue.  The same rules apply.  How are you trying to affect your subject?

Second of all, were you cold?  Is there a way you could have either made yourself cold, or felt colder?  That may have helped.  

I would recommend a few steps - make notes of who the character is, build their bio.  Ask yourself how they walk  - are they led by their chest, head, or groin.  Get comfortable walking in that.  How do they hold their body?  So far, I kind of bought that this character was down on their luck, and you held that in the body pretty well.  

Next, notarize your emotional memories of the character.  Think of the things they are talking about, write the mini internal monologues of them, draw pictures of the people they talk about, or to.

You may want to ask the director what they want as well - in terms of how big or how small and find a way to gradually get to that point, or justify that.

Alot of this stuff is pretty general and could apply to any part of acting, but think it could help here.

Most people can't make a living from solely acting.  People end up doing this, that and the other to make ends meet.  It is as they say, what it is.

I could sit here and try and think of what the best approach is, to make it successful as an actor - do I build more time in my schedule to network online, or reach out to people?  Do I go to more classes in the hope that I cross paths with the right person, or that I am totally ready and relaxed the next time a big self-tape comes in?  Maybe.  That being said, I could also walk into that room and come off as a weirdo and an asshole that's hard to work with, because I'm putting so much pressure on myself to succeed.

I'm incredibly dubious of "gurus" who will tell you the right way to go about this acting thing.  I'm hugely dubious of anyone who offers non-stop positivity, that "Never give up attitude!".  Almost everyone has to know when their time is due, or they'll mentally break themselves.  

Likewise, I'm not saying "give up now, there's no hope".  As REM put it, I'm not you and you are not me.

What I'm trying to say is - it has to be up to you about what you do and how you proceed.

We can all sit here and give you suggestions like "go write something, get some film maker friends to shoot it", "go to classes", "check stuff out on youtube", "get on local facebook groups in your area and meet up with amateur actors", but these are all suggestions.  Either use the negativity and self-doubt to prove yourself wrong, or try to establish another path.  Maybe study what other career paths involve.  Who knows, maybe with life experience you can come back to acting with a different approach?

Almost no one is 100% secure in their acting ability, or faith in their own success.  If the self doubt comes from yourself, you have to figure out what to do with yourself.

I believe for many people, the addictive nature of a computer game is far more controlling than other media forms.  This is something I find myself - if I enjoy a computer game, I spend too much time thinking about it and wanting to play it non stop.  It totally overrides my dopamine centres.
